@graph.headline: Prop Firm Drawdown Rules, Decoded
@graph.description: Prop firm drawdown rules decoded: daily vs maximum drawdown, static vs trailing floors, soft vs hard breaches, and what a breach costs before you trade.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between daily drawdown and maximum drawdown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Daily caps losses within one day (typically 4–5%) and resets daily; maximum caps losses over the account's life (typically 6–12%) and never resets within an account's life. Either can end the day or the account. See "The two floors, side by side" — the daily limit tends to bind first on a bad day, as a tendency from the relative sizes, not a measured statistic.

mainEntity.name: What is trailing drawdown, and why is it more dangerous than static?

acceptedAnswer.text: Trailing sets the floor at peak minus the limit, never moving back down, so profits tighten room instead of widening it. See "Static vs trailing" and the $108,000 peak illustration: a static floor leaves a growing buffer, while a trailing floor raises the bar after every good run.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between intraday trailing and end-of-day trailing drawdown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Intraday moves the floor on every tick of unrealised profit, including unbanked peaks; end-of-day moves it only on the closing balance. See "Intraday trailing vs end-of-day trailing" for the wording tells ("live/real-time" vs "end-of-day/closing balance").

mainEntity.name: Does the drawdown floor move down if I lose money?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A trailing floor never moves back down on losses, and a static floor never moves at all. See "Trailing drawdown" — losses only bring you closer to the floor, unless a firm-specific lock has already stopped the floor climbing.

mainEntity.name: Can I be profitable overall and still breach a trailing drawdown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. See the labelled 6% trailing illustration: peak $108,000, floor $101,520, pullback to $101,500 fails while still up 1.5% overall. Under trailing, distance from peak matters, not just profitability.

mainEntity.name: Do open (floating) losses count toward the drawdown limit?

acceptedAnswer.text: At most firms, yes, under the equity-based model — a wick through the floor ends the account even if price reverses. A minority of balance-based models count only closed trades. See "Do floating losses count?" and confirm your firm's measurement before trading.

mainEntity.name: What happens when I breach the daily loss limit — soft vs hard?

acceptedAnswer.text: It varies by firm and segment: hard closure ends the account, while a soft breach (mainly some futures models) closes positions and locks trading until the next session, with the account surviving. Never assume soft — confirm your exact account type and stage. See "Soft vs hard breach."

mainEntity.name: What happens when I breach maximum drawdown on a funded account?

acceptedAnswer.text: The funded account is closed immediately — hard closure is the norm for maximum drawdown. In general you do not owe trading losses beyond the challenge fee already paid, for ordinary losses (not legal advice; contracts vary). Whether accrued profits or pending payouts survive varies by contract and must be confirmed. See "What a breach costs."

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate my remaining drawdown room before a trade?

acceptedAnswer.text: Balance-based: balance − floor − open floating loss. Equity-based: equity − floor, with no second subtraction (floating loss is already in equity). Check daily and maximum rooms separately; the tighter governs. See "How to calculate your remaining drawdown room" — the balance-based example there is $5,000 room minus $1,200 open loss = $3,800.

mainEntity.name: How do I choose between a static and a trailing drawdown account?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choose on give-back tolerance and verified mechanics, not marketing. Static suits traders who want profits to build a permanent buffer; trailing demands tight give-back discipline. Tie-breaker: if you cannot state your firm's measurement, lock, and breach consequence in writing, do not choose trailing. See "Choosing between a static and a trailing drawdown account."
